The exception concerns complete direct awareness, which has degrees. A person may mentally represent a separate being without knowing its own self-awareness; only someone who directly witnesses it would know it in that way.

The example of someone healing themselves may be only a verbal objection: even when a doctor or medicine acts as an intermediary, the true source of the action may still be God. The note also explains the actual distinction between a healer and a patient: healing and being affected involve different bodily powers. — س قده

The commentator argues that every relation, strictly speaking, has two sides that are understood together, and so those sides differ in meaning. He refers the reader to the earlier discussion of relational opposition. — ط مد ظله

The author distinguishes between paired descriptions, such as “knower” and “known,” and the two reciprocal relations “knowing” and “being known.” The first pair need not involve a repeated relation or real opposition; the latter can be a relation the mind considers on both sides. — ط مد ظله

If two sides were opposed by their own nature, no separate proof would be needed to show they cannot coexist. Cause and effect, mover and moved, and ready and what one is ready for do not form such reciprocal oppositions as terms; their relation comes from dependence. Earlier and later are truly opposed, so they cannot be one and the same. — ط مد ظله

The chapter gives three proofs of God's self-knowledge: knowledge is a form of existence; every perfection found in an existent belongs to the Necessary Being; and a giver of perfection cannot lack what it gives.

This is a test for deciding whether something is a divine perfection. It must not require the special conditions of lower beings, such as matter, bodily extension, change, or composition. Some such conditions follow from others, but they can still be distinguished in thought.

“Complete knowledge” here means knowing the cause's own reality and what makes it the cause, not every feature and consequence of the cause. Knowing every effect would then be included in knowing the cause. Likewise, knowing an effect in all its details could reveal its cause. — س قده

If “causal aspect” meant only the relation between cause and effect, the claim would be trivial: neither side exists as that relation without the other. The author means what makes the cause bring about the effect. — س قده

For example, fire's basic nature is a cause of heat. The source of heat is present before the relation called “causing heat” and before the heat itself, so knowing that source reveals the effect. — س قده

The effect does not identify its specific cause. Its essence, possibility, or existence considered as related to its essence is too indefinite to do so; it points only to some cause. If we know the effect as a definite existence, we may know its constituents, but this is a kind of knowing it through its own reality, not through a consequence it causes. A specific cause, by contrast, brings about its particular effect.

The commentator holds that reasoning from cause to effect gives certainty. Reasoning from an effect to a cause gives certainty only when it proceeds from a common consequence with no separate cause of its own; otherwise it does not amount to a demonstration. — ط مد ظله

The author first says that knowing a cause is one way to know its effect, then adds that things with causes can be known only through their causes. The commentator says this applies even to immediate knowledge: the appearance of any effect already includes the real cause's presence, whether or not the knower notices it. He recalls sayings attributed to ʿAlī and al-Ḥusayn about seeing God through all things. — س قده

In a detailed account, God causes the many levels of existence in an ordered sequence, from the higher and nobler to the lower. In a more unified account, one act of divine outpouring encompasses all possible things at once, beyond time. Either way, knowing the one source entails knowing what proceeds from it. The author presents this as common ground among the different views. — س قده

This is directed at followers of Suhrawardi’s Illuminationist school, just as the preceding point addresses Aristotle’s school. If God's knowledge were identical with His act of creating, then His act would not be preceded by knowledge and would not be voluntary. A voluntary act, in the philosophers' account, is preceded by knowledge, desire, will, and power.

The ancient philosophers may have meant that God does not know other things eternally because no other things existed eternally. But that does not show that His eternal knowledge excludes them: the things themselves may begin in time while His knowledge of them does not. The author rejects the denial and says it is unworthy even of a wise person. — س قده
Most theologians hold this view, even if they avoid calling God's knowledge “universal” or treating it as something added to His essence.

This note attaches to the claim about things being known “in reality,” and points out that the sources describe two ways of speaking about their prior status. Some copies also give the total number of views as eight. — س قده

Another way to organize the views is to ask whether God's knowledge comes before things. If it does, it may concern all things, as in Plato's view, or only some, as in Thales' claim that forms exist in an intellect present to God. — س قده
The author adds that the Muʿtazilites themselves may not need a separate proof of God's knowledge, since they deny that His essence has attributes.

“Higher minds” here means the higher level of knowledge. But how is this view different from that of the Muʿtazilites? They say that essences have a fixed reality apart from all existence, whether outside the mind or in it. The view under discussion separates essences only from existence in the external world. Once we place them in higher minds, they have existence there. That seems no different in principle from our ordinary mental knowledge of essences that have no external existence.

The reply is that both views go wrong if they assume that a thing's essence has a reality of its own alongside existence. Existence is what is fundamental. An essence is considered a “thing” through the mind's way of understanding existence, wherever the essence is found. There are not two independent realities—existence on one side and the essence's fixed being on the other. Even when our mind treats them as two, the difference is one made by thought. Removing existence in a definition does not give us an essence that stands on its own: its being understood still depends on existence. What appears as a receiver and something received is, in reality, existence considered in two ways.

The author's immediate point, however, is narrower. The essences are said not to have their own particular existences, and he rejects the idea that their fixed standing can be wholly separate from existence. His answer will say that, although they lack their own proper existence, they are present through God's existence. If the point had merely been that an essence does not exist independently of existence, one could have replied that its presence through God is compatible with its having only a dependent, conceptual standing—just as when the thing has its own limited existence. We must not overlook that distinction. — س قده
The Arabic word translated here as “recoil” means to shrink away from or keep one's distance from something.
Ibn Arabi uses “Be” as God's word. In the Nahj al-Balāgha, God's word is also described as His act; that act is the existence that flows through things. — س قده

The reports about things praising God before their worldly existence describe them as existing for God, not as independent beings. Their praise in that state is their recognition that dominion belongs to Him. — س قده

This is the Ashʿarite position. In another discussion, Naṣīr al-Dīn al-Ṭūsī interpreted the claim that knowledge “follows” what is known as a claim that the two must correspond, with the known object setting the standard for that correspondence.

Here, by what is known first, the author of the view means an essence considered simply as what it is, apart from being made what it is by some added act. A thing's essential features are not put together by a further maker. By divine knowledge he means the simple, undivided existence of those things at the higher level, an existence that has no separate individual features of its own. To say that knowledge follows the known is to say that this knowledge takes on the distinction belonging to the fixed realities. Considering what a thing is comes before considering whether it has one kind of existence or another: we understand what belongs to it in itself before what belongs to it through something else.

The best answer combines both ways of speaking. What is known comes first as regards the distinct character that knowledge expresses. Knowledge comes first as regards undivided existence. And what is known comes after knowledge when it appears as a particular thing in the created world.

But why would the fixed realities choose darkness, unbelief, or misery? Everyone seeks what is good and what makes them happy, in every realm. The reply is that at the level under discussion “evil” is evil only in what the word means, not as a harmful reality actually existing there. Evil, in its realized form, is what opposes a thing's existence and well-being, while good suits it. There is no separate existence at that level for such good or evil to act in this way. Every essence seeks an existence here in which its own nature and what follows from it can appear. It does not seek to have that nature abolished.

Think of the letters alif and dāl. The straightness of alif and the curve of dāl belong to what makes each letter the letter it is in the writer's mind. When they are written, they must appear with those features. An alif is not asking to become a dāl, nor a dāl to lose its own shape. In the same way, the fixed realities appear according to the identities they possess. — س قده

Just as each fixed reality gives itself its own character, God's one command brings to light what is already implicit in those realities. God gives generously; each being appears according to its own nature.

The comparison is that God knows His essence, names, and attributes as they are, just as He knows the forms of those names—the fixed realities. It also invokes the principle that knowing a cause entails knowing its effects.

The author has argued that image-based knowledge belongs to minds that understand through concepts. In his view, separate intellects do not contain mental concepts in this way. The fixed realities therefore cannot be things existing separately through God's names; what exists in higher levels is the fullness of existence, gathered simply and completely. — ط مد ظله
“Common usage” here means the ordinary way theoretical thinkers use the phrase. The note is not claiming that philosophical truths can be established by popular opinion.
The author has now shown how his interpretation differs from the Muʿtazilite view. He will next show how it approaches the older philosophers' account.
This assumes the view, discussed earlier, that things are known in detail within God's essence. Without that premise, the Platonist would not accept the author's argument. — ط مد ظله
If the separate forms were known through other forms, the chain would continue without end. If each were known only through itself, God would not know it before it existed. — ط مد ظله

The union of intellect and intelligible has two senses. In God's simple, perfect knowledge, the One contains all intelligibles without division. In detailed knowledge, God's light is united with each known reality without leaving its own level.

The passage supports the claim that Porphyry held a serious philosophical view. It does not, by itself, explain how God knows things in detail before bringing them about; that issue will be considered next.

The forms are called God's “word” because they arise from His essence and disclose what is hidden within it. They follow His essence eternally; His prior will is His joy in Himself, which includes the will of all things as His effects.

The argument assumes that a thing may be known even when it has no mental or external existence, as the Muʿtazilites claim. The author must rule out that assumption before the argument is complete. — س قده

The objection assumes that God's eternal power must relate to each possible thing in its own external form. The reply is that the thing can be present in God's power through the form by which He knows and brings it about.

The criticism concerns the arguments taken together. To say that relations exist because there are real things from which we can understand those relations is hardly a strange invention. Many Muslim thinkers have said much the same thing. So that claim alone cannot be the reason for calling this view utterly absurd.

Perhaps the criticism instead refers to the idea that relations are like “the fangs of monsters”: things imagined but not found outside the mind. Yet when the author calls their existence “assumed,” he does not mean that the mind is free to imagine them without any basis. He means something like the way we speak of things in a general statement that remains true whether or not we are thinking of any particular example.

Once we consider a relation, it can exist as a distinct idea in the mind. Before anyone thinks about it, however, its existence in the world is simply the existence of the real things from which that relation can correctly be understood. Those things provide a sound basis for the idea.

Some descriptions, such as blindness, can be understood from one subject alone. Other relations, such as brotherhood, require two subjects. The relation between knower and known belongs to the latter kind.
God's power is actual, not a mere capacity waiting to act. The created effect may be potential before it exists, but this does not make God's power potential.
“From outside” means from beyond God's essence. Avicenna's account is that the forms arise from God, as an effect from its source, rather than being received from something external. — س قده

The author means an attribute that comes to a thing from outside, so that the thing already exists as a subject before receiving it. In that case, receiving the attribute requires a power to be affected; here that means matter. The resulting composition is therefore real, not merely a distinction made in thought.

One might object that a separate intellect also receives existence from its cause. Considered in itself it may fail to exist; through its cause it exists. Yet it is neither a body nor made of matter. This is no counterexample. Strictly speaking, a separate intellect has no essence distinct from its existence. Even on the common view that it has an essence, its receiving existence is not an external addition to a subject that already exists. It is not such an addition anywhere, least of all in an intellect.

Moreover, the intellect's capacity is only the possibility of its existing; it is not a material readiness to receive something. If God, whose reality is sheer existence, had such a receptive capacity, it would have to be a material capacity carried by matter; matter in turn requires a form. God would then be bodily. He is far above that. — س قده

“Universal” here means comprehensive and encompassing, not an abstract general idea that leaves out individuals. A single higher form can contain a whole kind and its individuals, as a species-form or a complete whole encompasses what falls under it. — س قده
The forms are not successive ideas that God thinks one after another. Their order is one of cause and effect, not time. — س قده
Avicenna considers whether the forms exist in God, in separate Forms, or in another intellect or soul. Each option raises the question of how God knows the forms themselves.
These beings are assumed to be free from matter. So placing them in the “divine realm” plainly cannot mean that they are parts of God's being or qualities added to it.

It means that they take on qualities reflecting God's qualities, while the limitations that belong to possible beings become absorbed under the higher rules of necessary existence. Matter, movement, and their consequences are what make a thing seem separate from others. These beings are free from those conditions.

That is why the author often says that the intellects endure through God's enduring existence and are without beginning through His beginninglessness. This does not contradict the spiritual teachers' claim that nothing besides God is without beginning, since the intellects do not possess an independent eternity.

If that is how we speak of the intellects, which are God's acts, consider how much closer His own qualities must be. A quality is more closely joined to what it qualifies than an act is to its source, even when the act is one of creation without matter. There is therefore no basis for the complaint that no one knows what Avicenna means by the divine realm.

If the forms exist in another intellect or soul, that being and its forms are effects of God. God must know that source and what proceeds from it. If that knowledge differs from the forms' existence, another form is needed to know them, and the chain begins again.

At first it might seem that Avicenna's argument must concern the thing itself: its knowledge of itself would have to come before it, so that we could say the thing was known and then came to exist. Its form would then be in some other intellect or soul, and the same question would arise again without end.

If the argument concerned only representations impressed upon an intellect, it might look equally damaging to Avicenna and to the view that the forms are present in God's own being. But on closer inspection, Avicenna's point is stronger. The forms under discussion would be things that exist in their own right. Their existence would therefore have to be preceded by knowledge. They would not themselves be merely known forms able to dispense with another act of knowledge.

Forms impressed upon God's being in the rival account are, by contrast, already forms of knowledge rather than separately existing things. Avicenna has treated the separate forms and their place in the same way. His objection resembles the one the author raised earlier against those who accept separate Platonic forms.
The chain would either circle back on itself or continue without end. Both are impossible.

By “relation” the author means a relation as one of the categories we use in thought, and by “cause” he means causation considered through such a relation. He is speaking about the condition that comes with the relation, not the true relation in which being is given or the real, dependent causation through which existence flows. God's existence is necessary in every respect.

A relation considered merely as a category is a concept drawn by the mind. It is plainly different from, and dependent on, the reality of the thing to which we apply it. We cannot treat such a concept as necessary in itself. Yet it may still truly describe a thing under one of its aspects. The aspect through which something is known is that very thing viewed in a weaker way. This is like calling a person “a father” or “a universal kind”: the description adds something to our way of thinking, not a new part to the person's existence. That is the sense in which relational attributes can be said to be “additional.”

The passage also accepts the philosophers' language of intelligible forms as following from the divine essence, and answers an objection: would that not join possible things to God? Properly speaking, what is possible here is only the relational idea of God being a knower. The forms themselves are necessary through the necessity of the divine essence, eternal through its eternity, and enduring through its endurance. This is an even stronger claim than the statement that the First Intellect endures through God, rather than through some separate act that keeps it alive.

The causal order applies to the chain of separate intellects, not to Plato's “horizontal” Forms. The note suggests that Plato's Forms might still reflect, in a secondary way, the order of higher realities. — س قده
Avicenna distinguishes between a form that could be understood and a form that exists as already intelligible. The forms from God belong to the second kind.

“Agency” can mean either the relation that exists after maker and made exist, or the source that brings about the effect. God's real agency is the latter and does not depend on the effect's prior existence.

By “renewed reception,” the author means that a thing must receive a change from something other than itself. If a feature followed from a thing simply because of what the thing is, it would not be a new reception of this kind.

By “through readiness,” he means that matter must take part, because matter carries powers that can become actual. Water receiving heat is a renewed change that depends on readiness. But the number four's being even is not a change that it receives in this way; nor is fire's being hot in the same sense. These features do not come from another thing acting through some material base. Even if we imagined four and fire apart from matter, their natures would still require those features. In such cases, saying that the feature “belongs to” the thing and saying that it “follows from” its nature amount to the same thing.
Bahmanyār's word “subject” can mean simply that the forms depend on God. It need not mean that God receives them as a changing subject receives an accident. — س قده
The author's point is that knowing God's essence and knowing what necessarily follows from it are not two events. The existence of the forms is bound up with God's knowledge of them.

Suhrawardī is considering several possible orders: the forms may come before their effects, after them, or together with them. The author says each option seems to create a problem unless one sees that knowing and existence are the same here. — س قده

Suhrawardī's argument would make God's essence, by itself, insufficient to produce external effects. The author accepts that forms are involved, but denies that this invalidates the account of the first intellect.
The first intellect can be established by several arguments, not only by the claim that one simple cause produces one effect. — س قده
A plurality of aspects does not license arbitrary effects. Each form is the source of what corresponds to it in the proper order. — س قده
If the forms are God's knowledge of things, then what exists in the world must match them. Otherwise, God's eternal knowledge would not be true.
The objection repeats the claim that having forms in God requires separate aspects of action and reception. The author restates it before answering a different point. — س قده

Suppose a feature necessarily belongs to something and comes from that thing's own reality, not from an outside source. Since the source gives rise to the feature, it cannot lack the perfection that it gives. The feature must therefore be present in the source's own reality, though it need not be present in the same limited way. The forms that belong to God's knowledge come from His very being. They are present in Him in a higher and more complete way. If their higher, unified level belongs necessarily to Him, how could that level involve either a possibility of not existing or a capacity waiting to be realized? Even at their lower, more distinct level, these forms have no independent standing beside Him.

The intellects brought into being by God have forms belonging to His knowledge, but in relation to Him they are like words whose meaning depends on something else. They exist through God's existence and endure through His enduring reality. If even these created intellects have no independent being alongside Him, this is still more true of the forms that belong to His eternal attributes.

The objection says one form would cause both the first effect and another form. A similar question arises for the first intellect, which causes both a second intellect and the outermost sphere. — س قده
The forms follow from God's complete essence; they are not additions that make Him more complete. Their existence is an effect of His perfection, not a perfection He receives.
If even separate effects do not make God more complete, the same is even more true of forms that are inseparable from His essence. — س قده

Avicenna's question concerns whether the forms' existence makes God know them, or whether God's knowing them makes them exist. The second is the right account, because the forms come from His knowledge. — س قده
God's self-knowledge is not caused by the forms. It is identical with His essence and is already complete. — س قده
If the forms' existence caused God's knowledge and God's knowledge caused their existence, each would cause itself. The author says their existence and being known are one reality. — س قده
The argument continues the same point: if knowing and existence were separate, either would need to come first and cause the other. — س قده
God does not learn about things from the things themselves. He gives them existence, and knows them as effects that proceed from Him. — س قده

Avicenna considers three readings of the claim that God knows things before they exist: He knows them while wholly nonexistent; He knows them when they exist, by receiving knowledge from them; or He knows them through prior forms. The first makes a nonexistent thing knowable, the second makes God receptive to change, and the third risks an endless chain of forms.
Relations, as understood here, do not need a separate maker or a receptive subject. — س قده
Descriptions based on relations or negation do not add a real perfection to God. The problem would arise only if an independent positive quality were added to His essence. — س قده
The main issue is not whether God can be called the “subject” of something in a loose sense. It is whether the divine essence contains a real multiplicity. — س قده
Suhrawardī's objection concerns the idea that God is the subject of many real, non-relational attributes. — س قده
If receiving means undergoing a change that depends on matter, then it requires a material subject. — س قده
The same problem would arise if the received quality came from another thing and made its subject more complete. — س قده
